note: A rub is the part of Carolina barbecue that people from elsewhere expect to be bigger than it is. The levels below run from what a whole-hog pit actually does outward to a full modern rub, and each says where it came from. Quantities per pound are this project's rule of thumb and are marked as such; the proportions inside each level are either a named pitmaster's list or a published recipe's own ratios.
carolina_note: At most whole-hog pits the meat goes on with salt and little else, and the seasoning that decides the flavour happens after the cook: the meat is chopped on the block and dressed there with vinegar sauce, and at the Skylight Inn with Texas Pete besides. A heavy rub is a Memphis and Texas habit that Carolina pits mostly did not take up. Start light. Season at the block.

meats.label: A whole hog
meats.note: dressed weight, the middle of the 80-to-180 range a pit cooks

levels.name: Salt, and that is all
levels.says: What most whole-hog pits put on the meat. The flavour comes later, at the block.

anchor.note: The whole-hog record has it: the meat is not basted before the flip, and a dry rub is something only some cooks use. The rate here — about half a teaspoon of salt to the pound — is this project's rule of thumb.

when: Salt the cut surfaces, not the skin.
Season for real at the block, with vinegar sauce.

levels.name: Salt and black pepper
levels.says: The next step out, and as far as a lot of pits go.

anchor.note: Two ingredients, in a two-to-one ratio by volume. The ratio and the rate are this project's.

when: Mix the two and put them on the cut surfaces.

levels.name: Ed Mitchell's four
levels.says: Salt, black pepper, red pepper, onion powder — the list a named Wilson pitmaster works from.

anchor.title: Ed Mitchell's rub
anchor.note: His article gives the ingredients and no amounts: 'His rub comprises salt, black pepper, red pepper, and onion powder.' The four are his; the proportions and the rate are this project's.

levels.name: A full modern rub
levels.says: Sweet, red, and a long way from an eastern pit — the kind of rub a competition cook carries.

anchor.title: Barbecue Rub
anchor.note: The recipe's own proportions, held exactly and scaled to the meat. It is not a Carolina recipe and does not claim to be.

when: Mix it all in a jar; it keeps.
Put it on a few hours ahead, or the night before.
Cook, then dress at the block if you are eating it the Carolina way.
